#66 This seems to be the right thread to record something about notation for coflare forms.

Here is a diagram of the 232^323 coordinate functions on T3R{\mathrm{T}^3}\mathbb{R}T3R (which generalizes to Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn and then to a coordinate patch on any manifold, but I only want to think about one coordinate at a time on the base manifold right now), in the notation indicated by Mike in comment #7, where we write the differential operator d{\mathrm{d}}d with a finite set of natural numbers as the index:

[\begin{tikzcd} {\mathrm{d}_{\varnothing}}x \ar[rr] \ar[dr] \ar[dd] & & {\mathrm{d}_{{1}}}x \ar[dr] \ar[dd] \ & {\mathrm{d}_{{2}}}x \ar[rr] \ar[dd] & & {\mathrm{d}_{{1,2}}}x \ar[dd] \ {\mathrm{d}_{{3}}}x \ar[rr] \ar[dr] & & {\mathrm{d}_{{1,3}}}x \ar[dr] \ & {\mathrm{d}_{{2,3}}}x \ar[rr] & & {\mathrm{d}_{{1,2,3}}}x \end{tikzcd}]

Although I didn't label the arrows, moving the right adjoins 111 to the subscript, moving outwards (which is how I visualize the arrows pointing down-right in the 2D projection, although you might see them as inwards depending on how you visualize this Necker cube) adjoins 222 to the subscript, and moving downwards adjoins 333 to the subscript.

I might like to start counting with 000 instead of with 111, but I won't worry about that now (although Mike did that too starting in comment #46). I'm looking at convenient abbreviations of these instead. Some of these abbreviations are well established: d∅x{\mathrm{d}_{\emptyset}}xd∅​x is of course usually just called xxx; d{1}x{\mathrm{d}_{\{1\}}}xd{1}​x is usually called just dx{\mathrm{d}}xdx; d{1,2}x{\mathrm{d}_{\{1,2\}}}xd{1,2}​x is traditionally called d2x{\mathrm{d}^{2}}xd2x; and d{1,2,3}x{\mathrm{d}_{\{1,2,3\}}}xd{1,2,3}​x is traditionally called d3x{\mathrm{d}^{3}}xd3x. These abbreviations also appear in Mike's comment #7, where we can also write d0x{\mathrm{d}^{0}}xd0x for xxx. Note that these examples are all coordinates on the jet bundle.

Another obvious abbreviation is that dix{\mathrm{d}_{i}}xdi​x can mean d{i}x{\mathrm{d}_{\{i\}}}xd{i}​x. There is some precedent for this at least as regards d1x{\mathrm{d}_{1}}xd1​x and d2x{\mathrm{d}_{2}}xd2​x in discussion of exterior differential forms; for example, dx∧dy{\mathrm{d}}x \wedge {\mathrm{d}}ydx∧dy can be explained as d1xd2y−d2xd1y{\mathrm{d}_{1}}x {\mathrm{d}_2}y - {\mathrm{d}_{2}}x {\mathrm{d}_{1}}yd1​xd2​y−d2​xd1​y (or half that, depending on your conventions for antisymmetrization). But d1xd2y{\mathrm{d}_{1}}x {\mathrm{d}_{2}}yd1​xd2​y can also be written as dx⊗dy{\mathrm{d}}x \otimes {\mathrm{d}}ydx⊗dy, and I'm not sure that there's much precedent for d2x{\mathrm{d}_{2}}xd2​x by itself.

What there really is no precedent for is something like d22x{\mathrm{d}_{2}^{2}}xd22​x. But I think that I know what this should mean; it should be d{2,3}x{\mathrm{d}_{\{2,3\}}}xd{2,3}​x, just as d12x{\mathrm{d}_{1}^{2}}xd12​x means d{1,2}x{\mathrm{d}_{\{1,2\}}}xd{1,2}​x.

Finally, d{1,3}x{\mathrm{d}_{\{1,3\}}}xd{1,3}​x also has an abbreviation that I've used before, as in this StackExchange answer; and which Mike used as well, way back in comment #1: it's d⊗dx{\mathrm{d}} \otimes {\mathrm{d}}xd⊗dx (or d⊗2x{\mathrm{d}^{{\otimes}2}x}d⊗2x to be even shorter). This is because the first (from the right) d{\mathrm{d}}d is d1{\mathrm{d}_{1}}d1​, the next would be d2{\mathrm{d}_{2}}d2​ if it were just ddx{\mathrm{d}\mathrm{d}}xddx (aka d2x{\mathrm{d}^{2}}xd2x), but the tensor product pushes the order back one more.

Except that that's not what I was thinking when I wrote that answer! I was thinking more like d2d1x{\mathrm{d}_{2}\mathrm{d}_{1}}xd2​d1​x (but not wanting to use the subscripts, since I hadn't introduced them in that answer). That is, I'm thinking of d1{\mathrm{d}_{1}}d1​, d2{\mathrm{d}_{2}}d2​, etc as operators that can be applied to any generalized differential form. They can't just adjoin an element to the subscript, since the subscript might already have that element. So d1d{1}x=d{1,2}x{\mathrm{d}_{1}\mathrm{d}_{\{1\}}}x = {\mathrm{d}_{\{1,2\}}}xd1​d{1}​x=d{1,2}​x, which is why d2d{1}x{\mathrm{d}_{2}\mathrm{d}_{\{1\}}}xd2​d{1}​x must be d{1,3}x{\mathrm{d}_{\{1,3\}}}xd{1,3}​x etc.

So here's another way to label the vertices on the cube above:

[\begin{tikzcd} x \ar[rr] \ar[dr] \ar[dd] & & {\mathrm{d}_{1}}x \ar[dr] \ar[dd] \ & {\mathrm{d}_{2}}x \ar[rr] \ar[dd] & & {\mathrm{d}_{1}\mathrm{d}_{1}}x \ar[dd] \ {\mathrm{d}_{3}}x \ar[rr] \ar[dr] & & {\mathrm{d}_{2}\mathrm{d}_{1}}x \ar[dr] \ & {\mathrm{d}_{2}\mathrm{d}_{2}}x \ar[rr] & & {\mathrm{d}_{1}\mathrm{d}_{1}\mathrm{d}_{1}}x \end{tikzcd}]

Note that there's no contradiction here with the notation in the previous cube! The rule is that di{\mathrm{d}_{i}}di​ immediately in front of xxx adjoins iii to the subscript set, while di{\mathrm{d}_{i}}di​ in the next position to the left adjoins i+1i + 1i+1 to the subscript, etc. So repeating di{\mathrm{d}_{i}}di​ (which you can also abbreviate using exponents) never tries to adjoin something that's already in the set.

At least, that's the case if the subscript integers come in weakly decreasing order. But what if we apply d1{\mathrm{d}_{1}}d1​ to d2x{\mathrm{d}_{2}x}d2​x; in other words, what is d1d2x{\mathrm{d}_{1}\mathrm{d}_{2}}xd1​d2​x? I think that the has to be d2d1x{\mathrm{d}_{2}\mathrm{d}_{1}}xd2​d1​x, that is d{1,3}x{\mathrm{d}_{\{1,3\}}}xd{1,3}​x. So to interpret the operator di{\mathrm{d}_{i}}di​ properly, you first need to first rearrange all of the individual differentials in the proper order.

The other direction is easier. To interpret dIx{\mathrm{d}_{I}}xdI​x, where III is a set of indices, as the result of applying some operations di{\mathrm{d}_{i}}di​ to xxx, each element iii of III is interpreted as di−j{\mathrm{d}_{i-j}}di−j​, where jjj is the number of elements of III that are less than iii. So a special case is that d{1,…,k}x{\mathrm{d}_{\{1,\ldots,k\}}}xd{1,…,k}​x is d1kx{\mathrm{d}_{1}^{k}}xd1k​x, as Mike used in #7 (but thinking in the reverse direction). But also d{1,3}x{\mathrm{d}_{\{1,3\}}}xd{1,3}​x is d1d2x{\mathrm{d}_{1}\mathrm{d}_{2}}xd1​d2​x (or equivalently d2d1x{\mathrm{d}_{2}\mathrm{d}_{1}}xd2​d1​x), where the d1{\mathrm{d}_{1}}d1​ comes from 1∈{1,3}1 \in \{1,3\}1∈{1,3} and the d2{\mathrm{d}_{2}}d2​ comes from 3∈{1,3}3 \in \{1,3\}3∈{1,3}, because there's 111 element of {1,3}\{1,3\}{1,3} that's less than 333 (namely, 1<31 \lt 31<3), so we use d3−1{\mathrm{d}_{3-1}}d3−1​.

In fact, we can define an operator dI{\mathrm{d}_{I}}dI​ for any set III of indices. Again, each element iii of III gives us an operator di−j{\mathrm{d}_{i-j}}di−j​, where jjj is the number of elements of III that are less than iii. (And since these operators commute, we can apply them in any order.) For example, d{1,3}d{2,3}x{\mathrm{d}_{\{1,3\}}\mathrm{d}_{\{2,3\}}}xd{1,3}​d{2,3}​x means d23d1x{\mathrm{d}_{2}^{3}\mathrm{d}_{1}}xd23​d1​x. This is because the element 111 of {1,3}\{1,3\}{1,3} gives us d1{\mathrm{d}_{1}}d1​ (since nothing in {1,3}\{1,3\}{1,3} is less than 111), the element 333 of {1,3}\{1,3\}{1,3} gives us d3−1{\mathrm{d}_{3-1}}d3−1​ (since {i∈I  ∣  i<3}={1}\{i \in I \;|\; i \lt 3\} = \{1\}{i∈I∣i<3}={1} and ∣{1}∣=1{|{\{1\}}|} = 1∣{1}∣=1), the element 222 of {2,3}\{2,3\}{2,3} gives us d2{\mathrm{d}_{2}}d2​ (since nothing in {2,3}\{2,3\}{2,3} is less than 222), and the element 333 of {2,3}\{2,3\}{2,3} also gives us d3−1{\mathrm{d}_{3-1}}d3−1​ (since $\i \in I \;|\; i \lt 3\} = \{2\}$ and ∣{2}∣=1{|{\{2\}}|} = 1∣{2}∣=1). And this is also equal to d{1,3,4,5}x{\mathrm{d}_{\{1,3,4,5\}}}xd{1,3,4,5}​x.

I don't know about these operators dI{\mathrm{d}_{I}}dI​ so much, but my intuition about coflare forms is largely based on the operators di{\mathrm{d}_{i}}di​ now. That's what I'm talking about in that StackExchange answer when I say that certain differentials represent velocities, accelerations, and so forth. There are potentially infinitely many different variations of xxx (although we only consider finitely many at a time in a coflare form), and di{\mathrm{d}_{i}}di​ represents an infinitesimal change in the iiith of these. And such a change can apply to any coflare form.
